Please read this carefully:

<document>
# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
I've read it carefully. The comment's empirical work is mostly valuable. It turns several concerns about the Halden pilot from suspicions into measured problems:
- the withdrawals were misdescribed,
- the manager-reported index runs high,
- actual hours fell much less than scheduled hours,
- real revenue fell.

Table 2's arithmetic checks out (95.1/0.8, 98.4/0.859 and 95.4/0.861 give +18.9%, +14.6% and +10.8%), as does the inflation adjustment (1.014/1.041 is about −2.6%).

The problem is the step from the corrections to the conclusion. "Entirely an artifact" is not supported by the comment's own residual, and it is contradicted by the randomised evidence the comment cites selectively. The issues below are in rough order of importance.

## 1. The conclusion contradicts the comment's own results

- **The residual is not explained away.** After every correction the authors can compute, a gain of 10.8% per actual hour remains. The only argument that it is spurious is the novelty claim (§6), which is the weakest part of the paper (see §4 below). The abstract's "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty" therefore rests on an untested hypothesis, not on a correction.
- **The data note contradicts the conclusion.** The data note says the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole." The abstract and conclusion then generalise to "reduced-hours schemes" in general. Both cannot stand.
- **The "burden of proof" cuts both ways.** "Entirely an artifact" is a positive claim, and the comment does not meet the standard it sets for the pilot. The same applies to post hoc reasoning: the comment dismisses the Varden meetings correlation as post hoc (§7), yet its own novelty argument is fitted to two survey points.

## 2. The Varden case-processing result is left out

The comment calls the Varden counter-stratum result "the most reliable finding in the literature." The same trial's case-processing stratum, however, addressed every correction the comment applies:
- randomised assignment, so no self-selection;
- output from administrative records, not manager ratings;
- actual hours from timesheets;
- a control group that also knew a trial was under way.

It found +12.5% output per actual hour, with output per FTE statistically indistinguishable from control.

This is the most relevant evidence against "entirely an artifact," and the comment doesn't mention it. It is also very close to the comment's own residual of 10.8%. Two very different designs converging on a gain of roughly 10–12% per actual hour is the most interesting pattern in this literature. At least over six to nine months, in work that is not tied to presence, it points towards a real effect.

## 3. Attrition is described but never quantified

- **The abstract overstates what was corrected.** It says "correcting the first three" problems gives 10.8%. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition is never adjusted for.
- **Revenue is not part of the per-hour gain at all.** So of the four problems said to "account for most of the reported gain," only two are actually quantified.
- **The scale of the bias is unknown.** Nine of 70 organisations is about 13%. How much their absence biases the mean depends on their size and how badly they fared.
- **What would fix it:** a bounding exercise. Assign the withdrawers a pessimistic output, for example 80 (no per-hour gain at all), and report the resulting range. Lee bounds would be a more formal version.

The finding that seven of the nine withdrew *after* the reduced schedule began, mostly over workload, contradicts the working paper. That is important and should be raised with the Halden authors directly.

## 4. The novelty argument is the weakest section

- **Energy is not output.** The argument infers a decline in productivity from a decline in self-reported energy. But the pilot's output index was collected monthly, and time tracking is continuous. The authors can test novelty directly: does output per actual hour decline from month 1 to month 6 in the 17-organisation subset? That analysis is what decides the question, and it is missing.
- **The extrapolation is weak and the arithmetic doesn't match.** A straight line through two points (0.61 at month 3, 0.29 at month 6) hits zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten." The trajectory is also clearly not linear: energy rose from 0 to 0.61 and then fell. Extrapolating it says little.
- **Other explanations fit the fade.** Seasonality, or workload creeping back into the remaining days (the +0.7 h/day in §3 hints at this), could produce the same pattern.

## 5. The hours breakdown in §3 doesn't add up

For the 27 time-tracking organisations, the comment gives:
- scheduled pilot hours: 32 per week,
- longer remaining days: +0.7 h/day × 4 days = 2.8 h,
- work logged on the day off: 1.6 h.

That totals at least 36.4 hours a week, not the reported 34.6. Measuring the +0.7 against baseline day length (about 8.06 h) gives about 36.6. One of these figures is wrong.

If 36.4 is right, actual hours fell only about 10%, and the per-hour gain shrinks further. So this isn't an error in the pilot's favour, but it needs reconciling before Table 2 can be relied on.

## 6. The record-based output measure needs scrutiny

- **Billable hours are a measure of hours, not output.** "Billable hours delivered" is one of the record types. For a professional-services firm, cutting hours mechanically cuts billable hours, so using it as output biases per-hour productivity towards no change. Report how many of the 23 (and of the 17) used billable hours, and show results without them.
- **Mixing record types.** Tickets, units, cases and billable hours have been averaged into one index. Show the composition of the subsets and the results by record type.
- **No uncertainty.** None of the estimates in Table 2 carries an interval or standard error, and 17 organisations is a small sample. The comparison 98.9 vs 95.1 (19 of 23 higher) is persuasive as a direction, but the size of the gap needs a CI.
- **Unknown sector mix.** The subsets aren't described by sector. If they over-represent professional services or retail, the 10.8% figure is weighted accordingly.

## 7. The meetings critique misstates what the Varden authors did

- **The data were not selected after the results were known.** Varden collected the calendar data in month six, at managers' request, before the nine-month results. And the seven offices were not "selected": they are all the treated case-processing offices.
- **The Varden authors already said what the comment says.** They called the analysis unregistered and insufficient to establish a mechanism, and they registered a confirmatory test.
- **The comment ignores the stronger evidence.** The between-arm difference (3.8 vs 7.1 hours of meetings) is a randomised comparison, which is stronger than the correlation the comment attacks. The Halden interviews also independently mention meeting cuts (47 of 58 managers).

"Should not be cited as a mechanism" is fair. "Post hoc account fitted to a subgroup" is not.

## 8. Smaller points

- **The revenue deflator.** CPI is a rough deflator for business revenue. Sector-specific output price indices would be better, though the direction of the correction is surely right. The Halden paper also had already noted that revenue "is influenced by many factors," so "misleading impression of growth" is slightly overstated.
- **Section 5 agrees with my earlier review.** Its point that the per-hour metric guarantees a gain is correct. The retail record-based figure (−11.2%) adds useful support. It rests on three organisations, so state that.
- **The recommendations are good.** Record-based output, actual hours, comparison groups, longer follow-up and analysis of all enrolled organisations are the right standard.

## Bottom line

The comment shows that the Halden headline (+23.4%) is inflated by roughly half or more. The documented corrections (§§1–5) should stand, apart from the §3 arithmetic, which needs fixing. The conclusion should be rewritten. A defensible version would say:
- the pilot's per-hour gain is largely an artefact of scheduled-hours accounting and manager reporting;
- a residual of about 11% remains in the subset with usable data, close to the Varden randomised estimate of 12.5%;
- whether that residual lasts is untested, and the pilot's monthly data could test it;
- in work tied to presence, reduced hours reduce output per employee.

As written, the comment does to the reduced-hours literature what it criticises the Halden paper for: it pushes a defensible but limited finding into a sweeping claim.

I can draft a referee report on the comment, write a short synthesis across all three documents, or sketch the novelty test and attrition bounds they should run.
